summary: The AP article surveys startups racing to build humanoid or human-centric robots, driven by the AI boom and labor shortfalls from declining birth rates. Most prototypes are still clumsy, but Agility Robotics' Digit is already headed to Amazon warehouses while Figure AI, Tesla, Apptronik and Sanctuary AI pursue different approaches. Founders and veterans say the market could be enormous, and that even failed humanoid research yields useful technology.
one_line: Startups including Agility, Figure AI and Sanctuary AI pursue humanoid robots to fill labor shortages, though most prototypes remain immature and Amazon is testing Digit.
key_facts: Amazon announced in October 2023 that it will begin testing Agility Robotics' Digit robots in its warehouses.
Agility Robotics opened an Oregon factory in September 2023 to mass produce Digit.
Digit currently picks up and moves tote bins; it has bird-like, digitigrade legs with an inverted-knee look.
Agility co-founder Jonathan Hurst calls Digit 'human-centric, not humanoid', emphasizing what it does over what it tries to be.
Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock said: 'we can sell millions of humanoids, billions maybe' if robots do work humans don't want to do.
Figure AI was founded just over a year ago, has raised tens of millions of dollars, and has only shown a 38-second video of its robot walking in its Sunnyvale, California test facility.
Figure aims for a commercial robot that can be 'iterated on like an iPhone', starting with simple uses such as a retail warehouse.
Tesla's Optimus humanoid had a live demonstration last year with awkwardly halting steps that did not impress robotics experts.
Apptronik, based in Austin, Texas, unveiled its Apollo humanoid in an August video demonstration.
Marc Raibert of Boston Dynamics said humanoid research led to a non-humanoid robot that handles boxes faster, works longer hours and operates in tight spaces like a truck.
Sanctuary AI's Phoenix, its first bipedal robot, can stock shelves, unload delivery vehicles and operate a checkout.
Sanctuary co-founder Geordie Rose said walking is 'not the hardest problem'; the hardest is understanding the world and manipulating it with hands.
Amazon's Tye Brady said 'The mobility aspect is more interesting than the actual form.'
Agility CEO Damion Shelton predicts that in 10, 20 years 'you're going to see these robots everywhere'.
